Prevention: Prune the canopies regularly to improve air circulation and the penetration of sunlight.
Remove fallen rotten fruits and fallen leaves from the orchard and bury or burn them.
Injuries caused by thrips create entry wounds and exacerbate scab development.
Add coarse organic mulch (composted yard waste) beneath trees and maintain the mulch layer 6 inches thick to help reduce the survival of thrips that drop from trees to pupate.
Encourage the presence of natural enemies (predatory thrips, green lacewings and parasitoids) by reducing the use of chemicals.
Monitoring: During cool and moist weather, look on young, succulent tissues of leaves, twigs and fruits for symptoms:
Small brown to purple-brown, oval to elongated and slightly raised spots with a sandpaper-like surface.
Eventually, the spots enlarge and merge, giving a corky appearance to the surface.
Fruit symptoms can be confused with wind damage and some insect damage.
Lesions less than 3.5 mm become necrotic and brown to black, often concentrated along leaf veins.
Leaves can become stunted, crinkled and distorted, and lesions may merge into star-like patterns and shot holes develop.
Twigs: oval to elongated, raised and corky lesions.
Leaves become resistant 1 month after emergence, and fruit become resistant once they are half-grown.
Direct Control: Remove scabby fruits from the orchard as they often become primary sources of inoculum the following year if left in the trees during harvest.
Remove dead branches and twigs from the orchard to prevent the disease from spreading as it can survive on dead material for a long time.
